stem: A client with lung cancer develops new facial and neck swelling, distended neck veins, and dyspnea. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
rationale: Superior vena cava syndrome results from impaired blood flow through the superior vena cava. NCI guidance describes dyspnea and swelling of the face and neck as characteristic symptoms, with neck-vein distention among the physical findings; bronchogenic malignancy is a common associated cause. The other conditions do not explain this upper-body venous congestion pattern. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Recognize facial/neck swelling, neck-vein distention, and dyspnea in a client with lung cancer as findings suggestive of superior vena cava syndrome.
source_document_title: Cardiopulmonary Syndromes (PDQ®) — Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
source_locator: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome → Overview: symptoms include dyspnea and swelling of face/neck/upper trunk/extremities; physical signs include neck-vein distention and edema of face/upper extremities; SVCS is usually associated with locally advanced bronchogenic carcinoma
source_claim_supported: Superior vena cava syndrome can present with dyspnea, facial/neck swelling, and neck-vein distention and is commonly associated with bronchogenic malignancy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: manage acute/life-threatening physical conditions; identify pathophysiology; recognize signs and symptoms of client complications and intervene; Illness Management/Medical Emergencies
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — superior vena cava syndrome / oncologic complication
correction_summary: Upgraded the source to NCI and removed unnecessary claims that SVCS is universally an 'oncologic emergency' and that symptoms must worsen supine. The revised item tests the directly supported upper-body venous-congestion presentation in a client with lung cancer.
audit_findings: A uniquely explains the combined facial/neck edema, neck-vein distention, and dyspnea in the stated cancer context. B, C, and D do not produce this characteristic upper-body venous obstruction pattern. No severity classification or unsupported positional qualifier is required. Direct Physiological Adaptation relevance remains.
